client: I've been really struggling since my sister died. Some days I can barely get out of bed, and when I do manage to go through the motions of daily life, I feel guilty for even pretending to be okay. Everyone keeps telling me I need to "move forward," but how am I supposed to do that when she doesn't get to have a future at all?
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a heavy weight of grief and guilt, and the pressure to "move forward" feels overwhelming right now. Would it be helpful to explore what "moving forward" might look like for you, while still honoring your sister's memory?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Honoring her memory sounds nice in theory, but it feels like anything I do just reminds me of what’s missing. Even little things, like seeing her favorite snacks at the store, make me feel like I’m betraying her by living my life when she can’t. I don’t know how to move forward without feeling like I’m leaving her behind.
therapist: It seems like these everyday reminders of your sister bring up deep feelings of loss and perhaps even a sense of responsibility to keep her memory alive in a certain way. What would it feel like to consider that moving forward doesn't mean leaving her behind, but perhaps finding a way to carry her with you in a new way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I guess I’ve never thought about it that way before. It’s just hard to imagine how to “carry her with me” when everything feels so heavy right now. I worry that if I start to feel better or focus on my own life, it’ll mean I’m forgetting her or that her memory is fading.
therapist: Your words show such deep care for keeping your sister's memory alive, and I hear how that feels tied to your pain right now. Could we explore together what "remembering her well" might look like, separate from the weight of grief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... everyone keeps suggesting things like making a memory box or lighting candles, but those things just make me cry until I can't breathe. It feels like no matter how I try to remember her, it all comes back to the fact that she's gone. Maybe I'm afraid that if the pain lessens, it'll mean I loved her less.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep fear that easing your pain might somehow diminish the love you have for your sister. Could we explore together how your love for her exists separately from your grief?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That idea makes my chest feel tight. The pain feels like proof that she mattered, you know? If I stop hurting so much, will I stop thinking about her as often? I'm scared that time passing will make everything about her fade - her voice, the way she laughed, even the memories that hurt right now.
therapist: Your love for your sister shines through so clearly, and I hear how deeply you're holding onto her memory through this pain. Could we explore together how the strength of your bond with her might continue to exist, even as the intensity of your grief naturally shifts over time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I’ve never thought about separating my love for her from the grief. It’s just hard to imagine those two things apart—they feel so tangled together right now. Honestly, the idea of the grief shifting scares me because it feels like losing her all over again.
therapist: I hear how intertwined your love and grief feel right now, and how the thought of that changing brings up fears of losing your connection to her. Would it be okay to gently explore what aspects of your love for her feel most important to preserve, regardless of how your grief may naturally change over time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what I'd want to preserve most is how she made people feel - her kindness that could light up a room. But that's exactly what hurts to remember too. How do I hold onto the good without the pain swallowing it whole? It feels impossible right now.
therapist: It's beautiful how clearly you can recall the warmth your sister brought to others, even through the pain. I notice there's something almost hopeful in how you describe her kindness—might we explore what it would feel like to let those happy memories exist alongside the grief, rather than being overshadowed by it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I don’t know if I can let the happy memories exist without them hurting. Every time I try to think about her smile or the way she’d laugh at my dumb jokes, it just reminds me that I’ll never hear her laugh again. It feels like the happiness and the loss are tied together too tightly to separate.
therapist: It sounds like the joy of those memories feels inseparable from the pain of her absence right now. Would it be okay to gently explore what it might look like to let both exist together, allowing the warmth of those memories to comfort you even as you grieve her loss?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I want to believe that's possible, but right now the pain just drowns everything else out. Maybe someday the happy memories can bring comfort instead of just hurt, but that idea feels so far away. It's like I'm afraid to let the pain soften because that would mean accepting she's really gone.
therapist: I hear how the idea of finding comfort in memories feels distant right now, and how letting the pain soften brings up fears about truly accepting her absence. Would it be okay if we simply sat with that tension together - honoring both your desire to hold onto her and your understandable resistance to this painful reality?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah... maybe just sitting with this for now would help. I'm so tired of people trying to fix my grief or rush me through it. It's just exhausting constantly being told there's a "right way" to mourn when all I want is for her to still be here. I don't know if I'll ever stop wishing that.
therapist: It sounds like you're craving space to simply be with your grief without judgment or expectations, and that what you're really longing for is impossible - to have her here with you again. There's such wisdom in recognizing that some things can't be fixed, only carried with care. How would it feel to give yourself permission to mourn in whatever way feels true to you right now?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
